transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because... honestly, it’s gotten to the point where just the thought of getting on an airplane scares me so badly that I can’t really brush it off anymore. I know, rationally, that it probably doesn’t make sense—I mean, I can tell myself all the usual things people say about flying—but my body doesn’t seem to listen to that at all.

When I picture being on the plane, it’s like this certainty hits me that the plane is going to fall. Not “maybe something bad could happen,” but this awful feeling like it’s going to drop out of the sky. And I know that sounds extreme, especially saying it out loud, but that’s what it feels like. It’s not just dislike or nervousness anymore. It’s fear in my whole body, and it’s strong enough now that I felt like I needed help.
Do you experience similar levels of fear or anxiety in other situations, or does this mainly happen when you think about flying?

It mainly happens with flying—or even just thinking about flying, honestly. I don’t have this same level of fear just going through normal life. It’s the airplane specifically. Like, the idea of getting on one now scares me so badly that even though I can sit here and say, “Yes, I know this probably doesn’t make sense,” my body reacts like it’s real danger.

It’s not just that I don’t enjoy flying or that I’m a little tense about it. In my head it becomes this feeling that the plane is going to fall. That’s the thought that comes up, and it feels so convincing in the moment, even when another part of me knows it’s not logical. So, yes, it’s mostly tied to flying.
Have you found yourself avoiding air travel altogether or making significant efforts to stay off planes because of this fear?

Yes. Very much, yes. I’ve avoided it to the point that it’s started affecting real parts of my life, not just vacations or little things. I’ve canceled clinic coverage because I couldn’t handle the idea that I might have to fly or be near that whole process. I’ve skipped medical meetings that I really should have gone to, because they involved air travel and I just… I couldn’t make myself do it.

And my family is in Honduras, so that’s been one of the hardest parts to admit. I keep putting off seeing them. I’ll tell myself maybe later, maybe when I feel more ready, maybe there’ll be a better time, but honestly the real reason is that I can’t get myself to the airport. Or if I do get anywhere close to it, I’m shaking, and I need someone with me—I mean literally holding on to someone the whole time—because otherwise I feel like I won’t be able to keep going.

So yes, I’ve been staying off planes as much as I can. It’s not a small inconvenience anymore. It’s changing what I do.
When you think about flying, is the fear always focused on the airplane itself, and does it happen almost every time you are exposed to the thought or situation?

Yes, it happens almost immediately, even when I’m not actually at the airport or anywhere near a plane. It’s focused on flying—on the airplane, on the idea of being in it—and my body reacts before I can really think it through.

Like, even if I just get an email about a rural shift that would require a flight, my heart starts pounding right away. My hands get sweaty, and I get this feeling like I can’t breathe properly. I’ll be sitting there looking at the message, and it’s as if my body has already decided I’m in danger. I usually have to close the email just to get a breath again or calm down even a little.

So yes, it’s not occasional. It’s pretty much every time something brings up flying. Even the thought or reminder of it can set me off.

latest_inference.note: The patient's fear is specifically and consistently tied to flying, with no indication of similar fear in other situations. The response is focused on the airplane itself and occurs almost every time the patient is exposed to the thought or situation. The avoidance behavior and physiological symptoms further support a specific phobia related to flying, narrowing the diagnosis to F40.2 (Phobia, specific, flying). Other anxiety disorders such as generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), panic disorder (F41.0), or unspecified anxiety disorder (F41.9) are ruled out due to the specific and circumscribed nature of the phobia.
